topic: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances
subject: chemistry

items.q: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?
items.correct: At its melting point, the same value as for melting
items.misconception: At its freezing point, a lower value than melting
items.why: Everyday language gives every change its own name, so students assume every name must come with its own number. Data books quote only two values and students do not notice that the other two are not missing. There are only two temperatures. At the melting point the change can go either way, and at the boiling point the change can go either way. Ice melts at 0 degrees C and water freezes at 0 degrees C.
items.random_wrong: At its boiling point, where condensing happens

items.q: Bromine vapour is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which change of state is this, and at which temperature does it happen?
items.correct: Condensing, at the boiling point of bromine
items.misconception: Condensing, at the condensing point of bromine
items.why: Everyday language gives every change its own name, so students assume every name must come with its own number. Data books quote only two values and students do not notice that the other two are not missing. There are only two temperatures. At the melting point the change can go either way, and at the boiling point the change can go either way. Ice melts at 0 degrees C and water freezes at 0 degrees C.
items.random_wrong: Freezing, at the melting point of bromine

items.q: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?
items.correct: As small solid spheres of the same kind
items.misconception: As spheres drawn to the true size of an atom
items.why: Diagrams are drawn confidently and to a neat scale, so students read them as pictures rather than as models. In the model particles are represented by small solid spheres. Real atoms are not solid spheres and are far too small to be drawn to scale.
items.random_wrong: As spheres that swell when the solid melts

items.q: A solid is heated until it melts. Using the simple particle model, what happens to the particles?
items.correct: They stay the same but move further apart
items.misconception: They soften and change into smaller spheres
items.why: Students transfer what they can see happening to the whole lump onto the single particle, so the particle is imagined melting too. Melting changes only the arrangement and the movement of the particles. Each particle is unchanged before and after the change of state.
items.random_wrong: They break up into several smaller particles

items.q: Substance X melts at 801 degrees C and substance Y melts at -7 degrees C. What does this tell you about the two substances?
items.correct: The forces between the particles in X are much stronger
items.misconception: The particles in X must be much heavier than in Y
items.why: Mass is easier to picture than force, and heavier objects are harder to lift, so students transfer that feeling to particles. The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, which depends on the type of bonding and the structure, not on particle mass.
items.random_wrong: Substance Y has no forces between its particles

items.q: Why do some substances need much more energy to boil than others?
items.correct: Because the forces between their particles are stronger
items.misconception: Because the particles they contain are larger and heavier
items.why: Mass is easier to picture than force, and heavier objects are harder to lift, so students transfer that feeling to particles. The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, which depends on the type of bonding and the structure, not on particle mass.
items.random_wrong: Because they have to be heated for a much longer time

items.q: (HT only) Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the three states of matter?
items.correct: The model shows no forces between the particles
items.misconception: The model draws far too few particles to be realistic
items.why: Students notice the obvious visual shortcut first, because the number of circles on the page is easy to count. The specification lists three limitations: the model has no forces, all particles are represented as spheres, and the spheres are solid. The number drawn is only a convenience of the diagram.
items.random_wrong: The model cannot explain any melting or boiling at all

items.q: (HT only) In the simple model the particles are solid inelastic spheres with no forces between them. Why does this make boiling hard to explain?
items.correct: Boiling overcomes forces the model leaves out
items.misconception: The spheres are drawn much larger than real atoms
items.why: Scale errors are visible on the page, while the absence of forces is invisible, so the visible fault is picked. If there were genuinely no forces between the particles, no energy would be needed to separate them and a substance would have no fixed boiling point at all.
items.random_wrong: The model uses far fewer particles than a real sample

items.q: Ethanol melts at -114 degrees C and boils at 78 degrees C. What is the state of ethanol at 25 degrees C?
items.correct: Liquid, because 25 degrees C lies between the two values
items.misconception: Gas, because 25 degrees C is above the melting point
items.why: Students use one value instead of two, checking only whether the temperature is above the number they looked at first. Compare the temperature with both values: below the melting point it is solid, between the two it is liquid, and above the boiling point it is a gas.
items.random_wrong: Solid, because 25 degrees C is far below 78 degrees

items.q: Substance P has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. What is the state of P at 20 degrees C?
items.correct: Gas, since 20 degrees C is above its boiling point
items.misconception: Liquid, since 20 degrees C is above its melting point
items.why: Students use one value instead of two, checking only whether the temperature is above the number they looked at first. Compare the temperature with both values: below the melting point it is solid, between the two it is liquid, and above the boiling point it is a gas.
items.random_wrong: Solid, because both quoted values are below zero

items.q: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C but chlorine melts at -101 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?
items.correct: Sodium chloride has strong ionic attractions to break
items.misconception: The covalent bonds inside chlorine break easily as it melts
items.why: Students know covalent bonds are the bonds in a molecular substance, so when energy is supplied they assume those are what the energy breaks. The molecules stay intact. Steam is still made of H2O molecules. It is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.
items.random_wrong: Chlorine has fewer bonds, so it melts a lot sooner

items.q: A student says that one copper atom is shiny, can be bent and conducts electricity. Why is this wrong?
items.correct: Bulk properties belong to whole structures
items.misconception: A single atom is shiny but it cannot conduct
items.why: Students reason that a material is made only of its atoms, so each atom must contain the material's properties in miniature. Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity arise from how very many atoms are arranged and bonded together. A lone atom has no layers to slide and no delocalised electrons to move through.
items.random_wrong: Only atoms that are inside a compound gain them

items.q: What does the state symbol (aq) tell you about a substance in an equation?
items.correct: It is dissolved in water to give a solution
items.misconception: It is a liquid, whether or not it is water
items.why: Solutions are poured like liquids, so students treat (aq) and (l) as interchangeable ways of saying the same thing. (l) means the pure substance itself is liquid, such as water at room temperature. (aq) means the substance is dissolved in water to form an aqueous solution.
items.random_wrong: It is the water used as the solvent here

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
items.correct: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
items.misconception: Mg(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
items.why: The metal is dropped into a solution, so students label it with the state of the mixture rather than the state of the metal itself. The state symbol describes the substance as it is at the start of the reaction. Magnesium ribbon is a solid, so it is Mg(s), even though it is added to a solution.
items.random_wrong: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)

items.q: Calcium carbonate chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
items.correct: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
items.misconception: CaCO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
items.why: The metal is dropped into a solution, so students label it with the state of the mixture rather than the state of the metal itself. The state symbol describes the substance as it is at the start of the reaction. Magnesium ribbon is a solid, so it is Mg(s), even though it is added to a solution.
items.random_wrong: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)

items.q: Why is sodium chloride described as a giant ionic lattice?
items.correct: Very many ions sit in a regular repeating pattern
items.misconception: It is built from millions of NaCl molecules joined up
items.why: The formula NaCl looks like the formula of a molecule, and molecules are the first particles students meet. In the lattice every sodium ion is surrounded by chloride ions and every chloride ion by sodium ions. NaCl gives the ratio of ions, not a molecule.
items.random_wrong: Every sodium ion is attracted to just one chloride ion

items.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and boiling points?
items.correct: Breaking the many strong bonds needs large amounts of energy
items.misconception: The ions are heavy and packed so tightly they cannot move
items.why: Close packing is visible in a diagram, whereas the strength of an electrostatic force is not, so packing is used as the explanation. The high melting point comes from the many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions. Breaking them needs a large amount of energy.
items.random_wrong: Every ion in the lattice repels the ions beside it

items.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?
items.correct: In the liquid the ions are free to move and carry charge
items.misconception: Melting releases electrons that can move through the liquid
items.why: Conduction is first taught for metals, where electrons are the charge carriers, so the same explanation is reused for every conductor. Ionic compounds contain ions, not free electrons. When melted or dissolved the ions become free to move and so charge can flow.
items.random_wrong: Melting turns the neutral particles into charged ions

items.q: Sodium chloride is dissolved in water. Why does the solution conduct electricity?
items.correct: The ions separate and are free to move about
items.misconception: Water itself is a very good conductor of electricity
items.why: Safety warnings about water and electricity teach students that water conducts, and the warning is remembered as chemistry. Pure water is a very poor conductor. A salt solution conducts because dissolving separates the ions and lets them move and carry charge.
items.random_wrong: Dissolving splits the molecules into atoms

items.q: Why are substances made of small molecules usually gases or liquids at room temperature?
items.correct: Only weak forces hold the molecules together
items.misconception: Their covalent bonds are weak and break very easily
items.why: Students know covalent bonds are the bonds in a molecular substance, so when energy is supplied they assume those are what the energy breaks. The molecules stay intact. Steam is still made of H2O molecules. It is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.
items.random_wrong: Their molecules are light enough to float away

items.q: When liquid water boils, what is overcome?
items.correct: The intermolecular forces between the water molecules
items.misconception: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
items.why: Students know covalent bonds are the bonds in a molecular substance, so when energy is supplied they assume those are what the energy breaks. The molecules stay intact. Steam is still made of H2O molecules. It is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.
items.random_wrong: Both the covalent bonds and the forces between them

items.q: Which statement about a substance made of small molecules is correct?
items.correct: Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds
items.misconception: Covalent bonds are the weakest forces in the substance
items.why: Students who have been told covalent bonds are strong still expect a share of the energy to go into breaking them. Boiling water gives steam, which is still made of H2O molecules. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are untouched.
items.random_wrong: Intermolecular forces act inside each molecule

items.q: Methane, CH4, boils at -162 degrees C while octane, C8H18, boils at 126 degrees C. Why is octane's boiling point so much higher?
items.correct: Its molecules are larger, so the forces are stronger
items.misconception: Octane molecules are heavier, so they need more heat energy
items.why: Mass is easier to picture than force, and heavier objects are harder to lift, so students transfer that feeling to particles. The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, which depends on the type of bonding and the structure, not on particle mass.
items.random_wrong: Octane has more covalent bonds that must be broken first

items.q: Why does liquid octane not conduct electricity?
items.correct: Its molecules have no overall electric charge
items.misconception: It has no metal atoms to carry the charge along
items.why: Conduction is first met in metals and in solids, so students rule out anything that is neither. Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. Molecules are neutral overall, so a molecular substance has no charge to carry, whatever its state.
items.random_wrong: Liquids are not able to conduct electricity at all

items.q: The bonds inside a Cl2 molecule are strong, yet chlorine boils at -34 degrees C. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: Boiling only has to overcome weak forces between molecules
items.misconception: The strong covalent bonds break as the chlorine boils
items.why: Students know covalent bonds are the bonds in a molecular substance, so when energy is supplied they assume those are what the energy breaks. The molecules stay intact. Steam is still made of H2O molecules. It is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.
items.random_wrong: Some covalent bonds break and some are left whole

items.q: Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature?
items.correct: Its very large molecules attract each other strongly
items.misconception: Covalent bonds join each polymer chain to the next one
items.why: Students know polymers are strong and that covalent bonds are strong, so the strength is credited to covalent bonds everywhere. Within a polymer molecule the atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. Between molecules the intermolecular forces are relatively strong because the molecules are very large.
items.random_wrong: It is a giant covalent structure just like diamond

items.q: A diagram shows a long chain of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with the chain continuing at both ends. What does it show?
items.correct: A polymer built from large molecules
items.misconception: A giant covalent structure such as silica
items.why: Both are drawn as large networks of atoms, and both are solids, so the two categories are merged. In diamond every atom is linked to other atoms throughout the whole structure. A polymer consists of separate long molecules held to each other by intermolecular forces.
items.random_wrong: A metal, since the atoms lie in a line

items.q: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?
items.correct: Strong covalent bonds must be overcome
items.misconception: Its intermolecular forces are very strong
items.why: Students learn that covalent substances melt at low temperatures because of weak intermolecular forces, then apply that rule to every covalent substance. Silicon dioxide has no separate molecules. All of its atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds, and those bonds must be overcome to melt it.
items.random_wrong: Strong forces hold its oppositely charged ions

items.q: A diagram shows every carbon atom bonded to four other carbon atoms in a continuous network. What does the diagram show?
items.correct: A giant covalent structure, such as diamond
items.misconception: A very large molecule of carbon, like C60
items.why: Both are drawn as large networks of atoms, and both are solids, so the two categories are merged. In diamond every atom is linked to other atoms throughout the whole structure. A polymer consists of separate long molecules held to each other by intermolecular forces.
items.random_wrong: A giant metallic lattice of carbon atoms

items.q: Why do most metals have high melting points and boiling points?
items.correct: The metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong
items.misconception: The atoms in a metal are heavy and packed very tightly
items.why: Mass is easier to picture than force, and heavier objects are harder to lift, so students transfer that feeling to particles. The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, which depends on the type of bonding and the structure, not on particle mass.
items.random_wrong: Metals are hard, and hard materials melt slowly

items.q: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?
items.correct: Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding
items.misconception: The two metals react to make a new compound entirely
items.why: Students expect two substances put together and heated to react, and the alloy has properties neither metal had. An alloy is a mixture. Its atoms are of different sizes, which distorts the layers and stops them sliding, so the alloy is harder than the pure metal.
items.random_wrong: The alloy contains far more delocalised electrons

items.q: Why are metals good conductors of electricity and of thermal energy?
items.correct: Delocalised electrons carry charge and energy
items.misconception: The metal ions are free to move around the metal
items.why: Conduction in molten ionic compounds is explained by moving ions, so the same explanation is reused for metals. In a solid metal the positive ions stay in place in the giant structure. It is the delocalised electrons that move and carry charge through the metal.
items.random_wrong: The atoms are packed so tightly that energy passes

items.q: A gas is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Is this freezing?
items.correct: No, it is condensing, and it happens at the boiling point.
items.misconception: Any change caused by cooling is called freezing, and it happens at the melting point.
items.why: Students link cooling with freezing because that is what a freezer does, so both cooling changes get the same name and the same temperature. Cooling a gas to a liquid is condensing and takes place at the boiling point. Cooling a liquid to a solid is freezing and takes place at the melting point.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does melting or boiling break the particles into smaller pieces?
items.correct: No. A change of state separates particles from each other; it does not break them up.
items.misconception: Heating a substance until it melts or boils splits its particles into smaller particles.
items.why: Both processes are described as things being 'broken', so breaking forces and breaking particles are treated as the same event. A change of state overcomes the forces holding particles together. The particles themselves survive unchanged, which is why the change can be reversed by cooling.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a substance boil at a higher temperature simply because it was heated for longer?
items.correct: No. The boiling point depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.
items.misconception: The longer a substance is heated, the higher the temperature at which it boils.
items.why: Students confuse the time taken to reach the boiling point with the value of the boiling point itself. The boiling point is a fixed property of the substance. Heating for longer supplies more energy but does not change the temperature at which the substance boils.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: (HT) Can the simple model explain changes of state at all?
items.correct: Yes, in part; it explains arrangement and movement but not the energy needed.
items.misconception: Because the model has limitations it is useless, and it cannot explain melting or boiling at all.
items.why: Once students learn a model is limited they treat it as wrong, rather than as useful within a boundary. The model explains the arrangement and movement of particles in each state well. What it cannot explain is why energy is needed to change state, because it includes no forces.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A substance has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. Is it solid at 20 degrees C?
items.correct: No. It is a gas, because 20 degrees C is above -183 degrees C.
items.misconception: Negative melting and boiling values mean the substance is a cold solid.
items.why: The minus sign is read as 'cold', and cold is associated with solids such as ice, so the negative numbers are taken as evidence of a solid. A negative boiling point means the substance boils far below room temperature, so at 20 degrees C it is already a gas.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should you assume a substance is a liquid at room temperature unless told otherwise?
items.correct: No. The state must be worked out from the melting point and boiling point data.
items.misconception: Substances are liquids at room temperature unless there is a reason to think otherwise.
items.why: Most laboratory chemicals students meet are in bottles of solution, so liquid feels like the default state. Always compare room temperature with both quoted values. Room temperature is just another temperature to place on the scale.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the difference between the melting points of sodium chloride and chlorine caused by the number of bonds alone?
items.correct: No. It is caused by the type of bonding and the strength of the forces to be overcome.
items.misconception: All bonds are about equally strong, so a substance with fewer bonds simply melts sooner.
items.why: Bonds are usually drawn as identical lines, so students count them rather than compare their strengths. Different types of bonding give forces of very different strengths. Strong electrostatic attraction in an ionic lattice needs far more energy to overcome than weak intermolecular forces.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does (aq) mean pure water?
items.correct: No. It labels the dissolved substance, not the water.
items.misconception: The symbol (aq) is a way of writing water into an equation.
items.why: The word aqueous is heard as a synonym for water, so the symbol is attached to the solvent rather than to the solute. (aq) is written after the formula of the substance that is dissolved. Water itself, when it is a product or reactant in its own right, is written H2O(l).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the water made in a neutralisation reaction labelled?
items.correct: As H2O(l).
items.misconception: Water in an equation is written as H2O(aq).
items.why: Students associate water with the symbol (aq) because (aq) means dissolved in water, so the two are merged. Water produced in a reaction is a pure liquid, so it takes (l). The symbol (aq) is reserved for a substance dissolved in water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is dilute hydrochloric acid labelled in an equation?
items.correct: As HCl(aq), because it is dissolved in water.
items.misconception: Dilute acid is written HCl(l) because it can be poured.
items.why: Students choose the state symbol by looking at the bottle rather than by asking what is dissolved in what. Dilute acids are solutions of the acid in water, so they always take (aq). Only a pure liquid substance takes (l).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is each sodium ion attracted to just one chloride ion?
items.correct: No. Each ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it.
items.misconception: Ions pair up, one positive with one negative, and the pairs then stack together.
items.why: Bonding diagrams show a single electron transfer between one atom and one other, so students keep those two particles paired for good. In a giant ionic lattice the electrostatic forces of attraction act in all directions between oppositely charged ions, which is what makes the structure so strong.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the electrostatic forces in an ionic lattice act in only some directions?
items.correct: No. They act in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
items.misconception: The forces act only along the rows of the lattice, like bonds drawn between neighbours.
items.why: Lattice diagrams are drawn with straight lines between nearest neighbours, which look like directional bonds. Electrostatic attraction acts in all directions around every ion. The lines in a diagram show the arrangement, not a limited set of bonds.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are ions made when an ionic compound melts or dissolves?
items.correct: No. The ions are already present in the solid; melting or dissolving only frees them to move.
items.misconception: Melting or dissolving splits neutral atoms or molecules up into ions for the first time.
items.why: Students connect conduction with ions and know the solid does not conduct, so they conclude the ions cannot have been there before. The solid is already a lattice of ions, but they are held in fixed positions. Melting or dissolving allows them to move, so charge can flow.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are substances made of small molecules gases because their molecules are light?
items.correct: No. It is because the forces between the molecules are weak.
items.misconception: Light molecules float away as a gas; heavy ones sink together as a solid.
items.why: Everyday experience of balloons and smoke links lightness with rising, and rising with being a gas. The state depends on whether the intermolecular forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together at that temperature, not on how heavy each molecule is.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are there any forces between the molecules of a molecular substance?
items.correct: Yes, weak intermolecular forces act between them.
items.misconception: Molecular substances have covalent bonds inside the molecules and nothing at all between them.
items.why: Intermolecular forces are not drawn on dot and cross diagrams, so students conclude there is nothing there. Weak intermolecular forces do act between molecules. If there were none, every molecular substance would be a gas at every temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does boiling water produce hydrogen and oxygen?
items.correct: No. It produces steam, which is still water.
items.misconception: Heating water enough splits the molecules into hydrogen and oxygen.
items.why: Both processes involve heating and both are described as things coming apart, so a change of state is confused with a chemical change. Boiling is a physical change that separates whole molecules from one another. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs electrolysis, not boiling.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do intermolecular forces act?
items.correct: Between one molecule and another.
items.misconception: Intermolecular forces are the forces holding the atoms together inside a molecule.
items.why: The prefix inter- is confused with intra-, and both words describe attraction, so the two are swapped. Intermolecular means between molecules. The forces inside a molecule are the covalent bonds, which are much stronger.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a larger molecule usually have a higher boiling point?
items.correct: Because the intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules.
items.misconception: Because a larger molecule has more covalent bonds inside it that must be broken.
items.why: Students correctly notice that a larger molecule has more bonds, then apply that count to the wrong forces. The covalent bonds are not broken on boiling. Larger molecules simply attract one another more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A diagram shows a long chain of atoms joined by covalent bonds, continuing at both ends. What is it?
items.correct: A polymer molecule.
items.misconception: A chain of atoms in a diagram must be a metal or a single small molecule.
items.why: Students match diagrams to the picture they saw most recently rather than reading the bonding and the continuation marks. Continuation marks at both ends show a very large molecule made of a repeating unit joined by covalent bonds, which is a polymer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is diamond held together by attraction between charged particles?
items.correct: No. It is held together by strong covalent bonds between neutral carbon atoms.
items.misconception: Giant structures with high melting points must be ionic lattices.
items.why: High melting point and the word giant are first met with ionic compounds, so the pairing is remembered as a rule. Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide are giant covalent structures. Their high melting points come from covalent bonds, not from charges.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do metals melt at high temperatures because they are hard?
items.correct: No. It is because the metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong.
items.misconception: Hard materials melt at high temperatures and soft materials melt at low ones.
items.why: Hardness and melting point are both loosely described as strength, so the two properties are treated as one. Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife yet still a metal with metallic bonding. Melting point depends on the strength of the bonding, not on hardness.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is an alloy harder than the pure metal?
items.correct: Because atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers, so they cannot slide over one another.
items.misconception: Because the alloy contains more delocalised electrons, which make the bonding stronger.
items.why: Delocalised electrons are the explanation students remember for metals, so they are used for every metallic property. Hardness here is about the layers. Different sized atoms distort the regular layers of a pure metal and stop them sliding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do protons carry the charge in a metal wire?
items.correct: No. The delocalised electrons do.
items.misconception: Because protons are positive, they must be what flows in a wire.
items.why: Students associate current with positive charge from circuit diagrams and conclude that the positive particles must be moving. Protons are held in the nuclei of the metal ions and cannot move. Only the delocalised electrons are free to move through the metal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do metals conduct thermal energy well?
items.correct: Because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.
items.misconception: Because the atoms are packed so tightly that energy is passed straight along.
items.why: Close packing is easy to picture, and it does play a part in non-metals, so it is offered as the whole explanation. In a metal the delocalised electrons move quickly through the structure and transfer energy, which is why metals conduct thermal energy far better than non-metals.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do a material's properties appear only once its atoms have joined into a compound?
items.correct: No. They arise from how very many atoms are arranged and bonded in a structure.
items.misconception: A lone atom has no properties, but as soon as atoms combine chemically the properties appear.
items.why: Students learn that compounds have different properties from their elements, and generalise this into a rule that properties come from combining rather than from structure. Copper is an element, not a compound, yet a piece of copper is shiny, malleable and conducting. The properties come from the giant structure of many atoms, whether the substance is an element or a compound.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.2.2 How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances
